Tidal interactions among galaxies are vital for understanding how large galaxies form and evolve. Utilizing an HST imaging sample of 100 massive early-type galaxies (with $M_{\rm r} < 11.1$ mag) from the HSC-SSP project, we quantified the prevalence of tidal features—including tidal tails, bridges, and rings—at redshifts $0.1 < z < 0.6$. These features, identified via visual inspection, occur in 19% of the galaxies in our sample. Our analysis reveals that tidal feature fraction (TFF) declines as redshift decreases, dropping from 27% at $z=0.4$ to 12% at $z=0.6$. We also found a correlation between TFF and stellar mass, where more massive systems tend to have fewer features. Assuming tidal features primarily result from recent major mergers, our data allow us to estimate the merger rate. The inferred rate is approximately $10^{-2}$ per stellar-massive galaxy per unit time at $z=0.4$, declining to roughly $10^{-3}$ at $z=0.6$. These findings align well with the predictions of the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model.

In my earlier work, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) was introduced, proposing a repulsive effect at short distances that contrasts with the conventional understanding that dark matter is needed to account for galactic rotation curves. This theory has been shown to replicate successful predictions from both General Relativity and Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND). Building on that foundation, this article examines the behavior of a perfect fluid in the equatorial plane and demonstrates that the fluid's radial outflow mirrors the rotational motion. Importantly, the theory predicts the flow will cease when the out velocity matches the speed of light $c$. Beyond explaining the observed bipolar outflows emanating from young stars, this research suggests a mechanism for understanding the accretion of matter into black holes.

Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are brief, high-intensity radio transients of extraterrestrial origin that exhibit variability on sub-millisecond timescales. While their origins remain a mystery, leading theories suggest a connection to compact objects, which would likely produce multi-wavelength emissions. This study reports the results of an initial search for optical counterparts to four FRBs detected by CHIME/FERMI, utilizing Swift/UVOT observations spanning ultraviolet to near-infrared wavelengths. No significant emission was found for the bursts studied, and we place stringent upper limits on the optical flux associated with these events. Furthermore, we address the limitations of our current data and outline prospects for future observations aimed at both constraining and refining theoretical frameworks regarding burst production mechanisms linked to these compact stars.

We introduce a unified framework for designing and optimizing active laser components, including the lens assemblies and mirrors essential for creating high-power laser beams for practical use. This approach enables the analysis of intricate optical configurations by applying a design workflow grounded in ray-tracing, wave-optics, and inversion techniques. It is highly adaptable for customization, allowing the modeling of specific issues encountered during laser optimization or when reverse-engineering existing setups. For power lasers, it is imperative that the focused beam exhibits focused power that remains invariant against fluctuations in the wavelength, beam profile, mirror/lens positioning, and source coherence. Our method provides an analytical solution to achieve position- and angle-independent focal spots characterized by minimal spatial intensity distribution. We further present optimization strategies for practical considerations, such as minimizing the physical dimensions of lens and mirror assemblies while maintaining focal spot integrity. We also address the challenge of "amplitude-to-phase coupling" in lasers; this phenomenon, where amplitude variations translate into phase shifts, is shown through the method to induce significant phase gradients across the focal plane that compromise the optical solution. Additionally, we demonstrate how the method can be applied to optimize the wavefront of laser beams by coupling wavefront control with the physical placement of optical elements. Finally, we describe a real-world case study applying this approach to the optimization of a 100 kW laser beam configuration.

Although GPT-2 and similar large language models excel at generating coherent text, they are text-only systems lacking the ability to incorporate visual cues, even when processing prompts that request responses to images. This study investigates incorporating visual capabilities into the pre-training phase of GPT-2 by examining various input methods for visual data. Specifically, we integrate visual controls using established joint training datasets for vision and language, such as VisualBERT's or CLIP-based approaches. Our experiments demonstrate that GPT-2 can be successfully transformed into a multilingual model capable of generating text based on both input text and images. Additionally, we showcase its effectiveness in zero-shot captioning, demonstrating that the model can create relevant text output for provided images without prior specific training.

Blockchain networks can support various digital contracts known as Smart Contracts; however, some users wish to keep their transaction details private. Concealing transaction details in typical blockchains is extremely difficult because blockchain networks inherently rely on public transparency. Bitcoin attempts to balance transparency with privacy through a variant called Ring Signature, enabling anonymous transactions. Nevertheless, critical flaws exist in Bitcoin's current implementation: first, revealing a set of ring signatures logically equates to revealing the entire subset of signatories involved, thereby compromising the anonymity of unrelated users who signed alongside them; second, validating these signatures demands considerable computational effort compared to standard digital signatures. This study introduces "Delegated Ring Signatures" (DRS), a new ring-based cryptographic framework designed to maintain user anonymity while enhancing transaction efficiency. Validation under DRS is markedly more expedient than traditional ring signature verification. Furthermore, DRS offers a solution that securely preserves anonymity even if a user is not the genuine signatory. We have implemented this protocol on top of the Ethereum network to create a testable model. Empirical results indicate that utilizing DRS could reduce gas fees for the most active transacting accounts by as much as 80%.

In the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) phase, the peak luminosity will surge to approximately $7 \times 10^{34} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, representing a 70% escalation from its design value and necessitating rigorous monitoring strategies. To enhance our understanding of this future lumerousity era and identify optimal tracking methods, we conducted detailed scans of luminosity parameters, leveraging data from 2018 and 2019 to analyze how the derived values correlate with the actual measurements recorded during those years.

This paper investigates $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ ($n=1,2,3$) decays with quantum numbers $J^{PC}=1^{--}$ and $G=-1$, utilizing an amplitude framework based on the hadronic loop mechanism. We demonstrate that the hadronic loop amplitude is dominated by $h_1(1380)$ resonances alongside non-resonant background components. Consequently, $h_1(1380)$ is identified as the principal driver of the decay process $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$, with branching ratios for the respective final states $\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$, $\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$, and $\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$ predicted to be $(1.00\pm0.04)\times 10^{-4}$, $(4.00\pm0.15)\times 10^{-4}$, and $(6.38\pm0.24)\times 10^{-4}$ respectively. These theoretical predictions are specifically designed for future experimental verification.

Training neural networks with quantized weights offers the potential to achieve lower computational costs and faster inference speeds. This paper introduces a novel optimization approach tailored specifically for quantized networks, introducing an innovative constraint framework. This method allows parameters to be annealed from the feasible to the infeasible region over time, guiding parameters gradually out-of-the way to the defined constraint boundaries to minimize objective loss. By employing a control variable that acts as a slack term, representing the extent of infeasibility, we formulate an augmented Lagrangian function essential for solving this constrained optimization problem effectively. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed optimization framework performs on iron network models of increasing complexity, showing superior results compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Continuum soft robots consist of flexible, continuously curved structures that adapt and change shape in response to external forces. Unlike rigid or semi-rigid counterparts, their soft nature and lack of distinct joints create significant mechanical complexities, rendering traditional control methods ineffective. To overcome these limitations, researchers have turned towards simulation-based modeling and predictive control strategies. While this field has produced a vast amount of literature over the last decade, the existing bodies of work are often difficult to locate due to their fragmentation across numerous journals and magazines. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the latest advancements in model-based soft robot control, covering both physics- and data-driven methodologies. By analyzing current challenges and future research directions, our goal is to serve as a vital resource that supports engineers and scientists in advancing the design and deployment of soft robot systems.

Recent research has demonstrated that breaking down large tasks into smaller subproblems via decomposition enhances performance in various natural language processing applications. This study examines the application of such a strategy to verifying tables, specifically focusing on validating the claims within them. We propose a decomposition framework for table verification that first isol distinct subtasks to assess which parts of a given statement hold true, and subsequently synthesizes their outcomes to deliver the final verdict. To realize this, we introduce DECTVER, a novel framework for table-based fact checking grounded in a contrastive learning architecture that functions by generating and executing multiple hypotheses for a statement's validity. Our model iteratively identifies the most suitable existing hypothesis among those it has encountered thus far, with each iteration focusing on a new aspect of incoming statements. Our experiments unfold in two phases: initial testing is conducted with a single large-language model to confirm the validity of our methodology, followed by expansion tests incorporating three diverse pre-trained models to evaluate broader effectiveness results show our approach surpasses existing methods, attuning accuracy of 92.80% on the Spider-FI dataset, as well as achieving state-of-the-art performance on both FIVER and TABFIV evaluation platforms.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a powerful class of generative models capable of synthesizing high-fidelity images across various resolutions and domains. However, current GAN architectures lack the ability to govern the specific characteristics of the imagery they produce. To address this, we introduce a method that integrates learned image attributes as conditions for the generator, utilizing an architecture where a encoder compresses both real images and network outputs into a latent representation. A discriminator is then trained to identify real images and detect instances where GAN samples fail to align with the provided latent conditions. Empirical results indicate that this framework successfully generates detailed images tailored to specified attributes and demonstrates an exceptional first-stage capability for tasks such as in-painting and style transfer.

We introduce a method to compute the single-time and single-frequency two-particle correlation functions for a many-body system across all times and frequencies by implementing the Fourier-Laplace transform on their joint time-frequency representation. Specifically, we apply this framework to a driven-dissipative system of bosons in a Hubbard model, where we calculate corresponding single-particle and two-particle correlation functions. By analyzing the connection between single-particle and two-particle correlations in both time and frequency domains, we provide a more thorough understanding of the system's dynamic and spectral properties.

This paper addresses the Dirichlet boundary value problem associated with divergence-form elliptic operators and linear or semi-linear variants including an additive or multiplicative drift in $L^2$. We establish sufficient conditions to guarantee the existence and uniqueness of mild, classical, quasi-stationary, and stationary solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under specific constraints, these solutions are differentiable, and we provide explicit estimates for their derivatives.

Many machine learning models struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, a process crucial for identifying when input data deviates from training sources. Gaussian Processes (GP) are a recognized robust OOD method by leveraging input data covariance to distinguish between training and test instances. However, their non-linear variants often underperform in this specific area compared to tree-based machines, while traditional GPs fail to capture complex input relationships. This paper introduces a gp Gaussian Process layer designed to learn non-linear input covariances, filling the performance gap where GP layers previously lagged behind tree architectures. We introduce two approaches for integrating GP layers into deep neural networks (DNNs): (1) pre-training GPs on raw data to establish strong baselines, and (2) fine-tuning DNs using GP layers to enhance both accuracy and computational efficiency. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods deliver state-of-the-art results across various classification and anomaly detection scenarios.

Periodically driven, isolated quantum systems typically evolve into an infinite-temperature eigenstate of the driving Hamiltonian, denoted as $n_{max}$, a phenomenon known as Floquet heating. However, recent investigations into periodically driven, open quantum systems have revealed the possibility of avoiding this heating over long timescales. This stability arises when system dissipation drives the ensemble toward a non-extensive steady state $n_c$ ($n_c < n_{max}$), effectively simulating a quasi-conserved particle number. We demonstrate that in such open and dissipated environments, this effective conservation law can be repurposed to stabilize previously dephasing modes, specifically a scar-like state characterized by quadratic excitation within a non-linear, many-body context. By driving optical lattice models under these open-system conditions, we observe that this scar-like higher-order excited mode can be induced to undergo Bose condensation at low temperatures. Ultimately, these findings offer a novel experimental avenue for generating scarred states and exploring their associated thermodynamic behaviors within perosnally driven and dissipated frameworks.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and its extended form, Software-Defined Networking for cloud computing (CSDN), facilitate dynamic network resource allocation to support emerging services like Service Function Chaining (SFC). A primary challenge in these fields involves managing interdependent computing and network resources under strict Quality of Service (QoS) constraints. This paper introduces a robust resource orchestration framework designed to address these interdependencies, minimize energy usage, and ensure real-time SFC requirements within fog-coupled CSDN environments. Our framework employs a hybrid strategy for resource allocation: virtual machine (VM) instances are hosted on remote data centers for energy efficiency, while buffer units for SFC support are placed at edge nodes to ensure low latency. Additionally, we incorporate a proactive and reactive approach, where fault prevention relies on monitoring system health and buffer utilization, while failure recovery utilizes historical data to optimize traffic forwarding, refresh buffers, and migrate VMs. Experimental findings confirm that this strategy not only significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in energy savings but also reliably guarantees QoS standards.

Loss functions are fundamental to machine learning, serving as assessment metrics that guide model training. While numerous approaches have been introduced to resolve specific issues, no single method universally addresses all challenges. This study employs the Gradient Surgery framework to investigate existing solutions and their effects on a model's training dynamics, thereby offering an actionable path for creating effective loss functions by explicitly analyzing the contributions of different design choices and identifying which are most influential.

We examine a specific class of holographic quantum error-correcting codes (QECC) termed hyper-invariant Mereas (hyper-Imeras), which are constructed within the hyperbolic bulk using a hyperbolic Majorana fermion network (hyper-Imeras). Similar to standard Mereas, these codes function as approximate holographic error-correcting codes where any approximate quantum information recovery can be achieved through an efficient local map in AdS/CFT. However, unlike conventional Mereas that require vanishing boundary curvature, hyper-Ineras are capable of maintaining non-trivial, scale-invariant correlations characterized by exponential decay, which depend on the scalar curvature. These correlations arise from a vanishing AdS dimension. We present an initial investigation of these codes by deriving their AdS bulk/CT duality and demonstrating that hyper-Ineras can be embedded into a hyperbolic extension of a holographic code. We also explore the duality between hyperbolic bulk geometries and boundary quantum systems, and discuss potential generalizations of the hyperbolic Imeras to other holographic codes with non-trivial boundary curvature.

Galactic center filaments represent a distinct, luminous, and compact class of infrared sources, with their origin and formation mechanisms remaining elusive. This study examines the spacing between adjacent Galactic Center filaments, specifically between G20 and G21, and the Non-Detection (ND) region toward the south of G20. Analysis of the spatial distribution of these features reveals that the separation distances follow a log-normal pattern. This finding remains consistent even when the sample is expanded to include sub-millimeter observations from the SHiNE survey. Furthermore, the spacing distribution of the eastern filaments along the central bar aligns with log-normal expectations. These results support a scenario where Galactic center filaments originate from a Poissonian process, potentially indicating a formation mechanism that is independent of the local environment.

In distribution networks, low voltage levels below standard thresholds often indicate high power loss and poor load patterns, but rising low voltages can be addressed using Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR). This strategy lowers voltage levels strategically below nominal levels to proportionally reduce power consumption, offering an energy conservation measure. The primary obstacle to implementing CVC widely is the lack of a centralized method for determining optimal settings across extensive networks. This research introduces "distributed optimal CVR," a novel methodology that coordinates voltage reduction levels between primary and secondary distribution tiers. The approach utilizes a model predictive distributed quadratic programming (M-P-DQP) framework that merges distributed optimization algorithms with model-based control, enabling optimization engines located at strategic nodes rather than a central hub. The method explicitly captures the complex, non-linear, and time-varying interconnections between primary and secondary distribution levels. Validated through simulations on a representative test feeder, the study demonstrates that this strategy effectively optimizes voltage reduction settings while preserving total power consumption.

We investigate a nonstochastic bandit setting where delays are assumed to be vector assignments associated with each arm. While an pulled arm remains hidden due to a random delay from the perspective of the bandit, this delay is pre-determined by that specific arm. Although standard delay-free models have been extended to time-varying or stochastic delay scenarios through various approaches, our focus addresses the previously unexplored case of arm-specific random delays. We introduce a new problem variation and conduct a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the standard $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{t})$ regret bound is unattainable for both general and symmetric delay configurations. In contrast, we present algorithms that achieve tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{t})$ regret bounds for a restricted class of delay patterns and extend these results to the more complex scenario involving groups of delayed arms. Additionally, we propose a novel method for bandits operating under unknown delay distributions and successfully apply this framework to the study of lagged experts.

Dialogue-based text generation aims to produce human-like interactions involving sequences of open-ended dialogues. This study presents the Dialogue Learning and Human Emulation Robot Emulation and Text-based Human Emulation (LEATHER), a unified learning-to-reinforce framework designed to handle dialogue generation tasks without predefined rewards. Within this environment, a learning agent builds a dialogue policy to maximize dialogue quality scores (such as coherence, topicality, and meaningfulness) evaluated by an external dialogue evaluator. This agent then leveriles the acquired policy to generate synthetic dialogue datasets, enabling the iterative refinement of its approach to improve upon future generations. Our method was tested on the multi-turn, topic-unspecific conversation task, demonstrating that LEATHER rapidly produces data that indigenously rivals human-generated outputs even when the analytical grading function is imperfect. This simple and efficient strategy effectively synthesizes extensive synthetic datasets suitable for large-scale training in open-domain conversations.

We analyze how these factors collectively shape the equation of state for quark-gluon systems. Site-specific loads on offshore wind turbines arise from the combined effects of atmospheric winds, oceanic environmental and operational conditions, and the physical site layout. To accurately account for all variables, state-of-the-art deterministic load simulations incorporate both the spatial and temporal stochasticity of winds alongside load and stochastic wind characterization. We propose a novel data-driven technique that models time histories of structural loads along a single-degree-of-freedom offshore wind turbine using Gaussian processes (GP). This approach combines GP with a hierarchical modeling strategy to create a probabilistic surrogate for standard deterministic simulations. The method's accuracy is validated using long-term, long-duration simulations of Moog, North Sea. Modeling the wind input first, we subsequently predict structural loads, accounting for uncertainty, by updating the wind-driven load distributions. This demonstrates that our approach can accurately model the extreme loads and wind speed distributions observed in the Moog, North Sea.

Turkey, known for its numerous natural hazards, recently experienced a severe earthquake with a magnitude of 7.5 in IZMIR. This disaster resulted in over 400 fatalities and substantial infrastructure damage. Social media, particularly Twitter, is increasingly regarded as a valuable tool for disaster relief and post-quake recovery. By analyzing Twitter data, authorities can gauge the scale of impact, pinpoint affected areas, and assess public sentiment. Automating this process through data mining and machine learning has become a necessary approach, as the vast volume of Twitter streams makes manual analysis unfeasible. Consequently, this study employs a data mining workflow to examine the Twitter activity surrounding the IZMIR earthquake.

The study utilizes a forward-optimization framework founded on the trajectory basis to investigate time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-PE). This approach addresses specific limitations of traditional methods, which typically rely on linear inverse problems, by achieving robust reconstruction of complex multi-dimensional trajectories in a low-dimensional space. Specifically, we showcase a Trajectory Bounded, Sparsity-Enhanced (TBSE) algorithm that facilitates the recovery of time-resolved quantum states from experimental TR-PE datasets. This TBSE methodology demonstrates the accurate reconstruction of multi-excitonic photoexcited states (such as those in the F2 molecule) from synthetic data and performs a detailed analysis identifying excited states (such as those in solid-state materials like NiO) using real data. Ultimately, TBSE establishes itself as a powerful tool for mapping the non-linear, ultrafast evolution of the electronic structure within complex quantum systems.

This study introduces SceNDD, a naturalistic driving dataset focused on scenarios, featuring over 1,000 hours of recorded driving across 15 locations in Germany. The dataset encompasses 728 carefully crafted driving scenarios encompassing 358 distinct scenario types. Vehicle telemetry for all participants is captured throughout every phase of each scenario: the initial briefing phase, the execution phase where the driver performs the task while subsequently being shown a debriefing phase after. Participant behaviors during these phases are analyzed, with the aim of evaluating how much an agent speaks and how often it makes mistakes during both the pre-drive briefing phase versus the actual driving phase versus post-drive phase. The results indicate that while talkativeness varies significantly based on driver characteristics and specific scenario parameters, most drivers demonstrate low error rates overall and tend to improve their performance as they gain familiarity with a particular task and setting. The dataset, tools, and analytical approaches provided herein are intended to facilitate the development of advanced driving simulations, ensuring they incorporate realistic human behaviors characterized by diverse verbosity levels and varying error frequencies.

Boundary Conformal Field (BCFT) and Interface Conformal Field (ICFT) theories serve as fundamental components of the broader framework of Conformal Field Theories (CFTs), particularly in the study of higher-dimensional variants. This research extends the concept of reflected entropy to contexts featuring interfaces and boundaries. Specifically, we demonstrate that reflected entropy can effectively quantify the mutual entropy between regions separated by a domain wall within an intermediate interface phase. Furthermore, we examine several higher-dimensional interface models to illustrate these extended principles. We also investigate the constraints faced by reflected entropy in boundary states, particularly concerning the reversal of strong subadditivity and the monotonicity observed in boundary regions. These insights collectively advance our understanding of entropic behaviors essential to quantum information and quantum gravity.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) have garnered significant attention due to their cost-effective and energy-efficient ability to manipulate radio wave propagation, offering substantial potential within 6G wireless networks. Despite contributions from researchers, most prior studies rely on the Common Pilot (CP) exceeding the RIS round-trip delay and assume ideal hardware conditions. This paper introduces an enhanced channel estimation technique tailored for coherent orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems utilizing pilot signals that fall short of the round-trip delay, while accounting for non-ideal, imperfect hardware conditions. By leveraging the linearity of RIS and the inherent noise resistance advantages of Extreme Learning Machines (ELMs)—a type of neural network—we propose a scheme that first obtains an initial channel estimate using the enhanced method and then refines it to approach the round-trip delay. The proposed method is evaluated against the Round-Travel Delay-Mismatch (RTDM) case, with theoretical analysis confirming the estimator's convergence properties. Monte-Carlo simulations further substantiate the effectiveness of the enhanced channel estimator.

This study extends the projective Free Energy (FE) theorem and Integral Fluctuation (IF) theorem for systems employing continuous energy measurements. We demonstrate that when the system's eigenstates remain constant throughout an infinitesimal time interval $\delta t$ and energy is measured via total Hamiltonian eigenvalues, the projective FE relation emerges from the IF theorem. Furthermore, by formulating IF theorems for arbitrary continuous measurements, we prove that thermodynamic inequalities associated with arbitrary Hamiltonians relax as measurement granularity becomes continuous. We also reveal that when time $\delta t$ approaches zero, the projective IF theorem reverts to the First Law within the framework of Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics (NET). Additionally, the authors have constructed an experimental setup to empirically demonstrate these newly derived thermodynamic relations.

In addition, the study investigates the deformation of G2-instantans on a nearly G2 manifold. The results show that for this type of manifold, G2-instantans are discrete, meaning there are no continuous deformations possible. The current global landscape has been defined by the Coronavirus Disease (COVID-19) pandemic, which has resulted in over 100 million confirmed cases and the death of more than 2.3 million individuals. In an effort to curb the virus's spread, many nations have implemented contact tracing initiatives aimed at identifying and isolating individuals exposed to the disease. While digital solutions utilizing GPS data, Bluetooth signals, and user-provided information offer a promising alternative to traditional manual methods, they have raised significant privacy concerns. This study evaluates the privacy metrics of various real-world and prototype location privacy-preserving protocols, covering user anonymization, system un-linkability, and user location protection. The findings indicate that generic digital solutions are vulnerable to attacks that could reveal precise locations of infected or at-risk individuals. Conversely, the proposed user anonymization and location privacy mechanisms can effectively mitigate these risks.

Investigating whether quantum systems can host quantum information remains a significant unresolved issue. Although current understanding is limited, it is evident that biological environments operate in a warm, wet, and noisy setting, leading most to conclude that any quantum coherence quickly degrades. Nevertheless, because biological processes occur at such a microscopic scale, there exists some evidence suggesting the feasibility of quantum information, whether entangled or coherently interacting, being retained for a brief period. This article reviews the current state of knowledge regarding the occurrence and durability of quantum coherence within biological and neural contexts. Furthermore, the article discusses the emerging quantum algorithms designed specifically for neural networks, emphasizing their potential to deliver a quantum computational advantage.

End-to-end encryption is a standard and vital attribute of contemporary messaging applications. To guarantee true end-to-end protection, encryption keys must remain confidential from all users, signal administrators inclusive, unless explicitly authorized. To circumvent social stigma surrounding strong authentication, the signaling protocol employs Personal Identifiers (PINs)—a temporary, non-essential PIN designed solely to verify connection integrity between participants over brief intervals, not for secure data transmission. This PIN functions as a verification code that changes frequently between chats, making it a prime candidate for raising user comprehension regarding its usage. However, this research reveals that most Signal enthusiasts and casual practitioners alike demonstrate a poor grasp of PIN functionality and associated security protocols, frequently believing it serves a much broader role than it does, including the belief that it is essential to secure the message body.

Its robust versatility accommodates arbitrary sites, equipment configurations, tilt angles, orientations, and environmental conditions, with optimal quadrature order selection guaranteeing accurate outcomes. The findings align closely with numerical integration benchmarks, confirming its reliability in modeling solar-power integration across diverse solar-power profiles.

The generalized Gauss-Newton (GGS) algorithm has become a cornerstone for large-scale non-linear least squares problems, particularly in machine learning for its ability to expedite model training by approximating the Hessian. Despite this efficiency, it suffers from high memory consumption due to the full-rank nature of this approximation, necessitating sparse or low-rank variants that introduce their own drawbacks, such as the need for tuning parameters or incurring significant communication overhead during updates. In this paper, we propose ViViT, a novel village-like structure inspired by the low-rank characteristics of GGS in the Hessian matrix under specific assumptions. By utilizing iterative refinement to access this curvature information, we achieve a fully batch-compatible framework that requires no hyperparameter adjustments. Furthermore, we demonstrate a theoretical linear speedup with the problem's dimension. Empirical results show that ViViT offers a compelling balance between the trade-offs among computational efficiency, communication costs, and convergence performance.

Object pose estimation is a critical component of object manipulation tasks, yet it remains a long-standing challenge due to scarcity of data and a divide between known categories and zero-shot targets. While prior research has largely focused on known categories, our study introduces a new dataset and framework for unknown categories. Using the new HighPose dataset, our method employs an enhanced training strategy to significantly boost performance. Furthermore, we develop a new learning approach that leverages rich textual descriptions to overcome data limitations. Experiments demonstrate that our model attains state-of-the-art accuracy, achieving a mean average precision (MAP) of 20.2% on HighPose even under difficult zero-shot conditions.

Accurate traffic forecasting serves as a critical component of intelligent transportation systems, yet most existing models rely on dense historical traffic data that is unavailable for the majority of road networks. This study, which employs similarity metrics to process large-scale sparse data, introduces a novel framework that processes data in three stages. First, it constructs a dynamic traffic state matrix by aggregating diverse data sources to build a robust baseline for flow prediction. Second, it identifies similar historical days to transform time-series data into time-invariant features, effectively removing the need for models to account for time-of-day variations. Third, utilizing these derived features, it predicts flow rates for future time intervals. Extensive experiments across large, real-world datasets containing more than 300,000 roads and over 30,000 stations demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves significant accuracy gains compared to state-of-the-art sparse and dense forecasting models. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/zhengyongchen/TrafficForecasting.

As micro- and nanophotonic devices shrink in scale, their dimensions become approachable to the wavelengths of incident light, causing light-matter interactions to become significant. This phenomenon, known as metaphotonics, integrates both microscale and nanoscale effects to exploit the dynamic response of materials and the static or quasi-static properties of circuits for controlling light. Although metaphotonics offers a versatile toolbox for developing sophisticated opto-electronic systems, translating these advanced concepts into practical, low-cost, and compact devices remains difficult. Consequently, this paper reviews machine learning strategies that capitalize on the specific metaphotonic characteristics which traditional photovoltaic concepts overlook. By exploring concepts ranging from microscale and nanoscale phenomena through to the dynamic behavior of metamaterials, this work outlines machine learning frameworks capable of addressing current hurdles in metaphotonics. Specifically, these include the difficulty in fabricating complex nanostructures, the need for real-time operation, and the optimization of intricate opto-electronic systems. Finally, representative applications and future directions for further research are presented to highlight the promising integration of machine learning within the field of metaphotonics.

This study analyzes frequency and voltage secondary control in inverter-based microgrids that rely on local measurements. Our findings indicate that with distributed power regulation, these systems inherently possess inexact load-flow outcomes that fail to fully balance power; however, the scale of this imbalance is inversely proportional to the secondary control loop's speed. Consequently, the residual power mismatch drives persistent low-dynamic voltage and frequency oscillations. While we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for global asymptotic stability regarding the resulting steady-state dynamics, our analysis also identifies scenarios where no such stable equilibrium exists. Inflection points, specifically derived from the frequency-voltage characteristics of inverters, are critical in determining the system's maximum tolerance for power imbalance. Remarkably, this threshold is also the tipping mechanism for stability loss. Leveraging Lyapunov methods, we develop a potential function to formulate practical, implementable stability criteria.

In summary, this research demonstrates that inverter-based invertor systems utilize distributed power regulation to avoid full power balance rather than achieving perfect equilibrium, leading to continuous oscillatory behavior. However, if the secondary control loop operates sufficiently rapidly, global stability is maintained. Our method establishes the specific conditions for achieving these results, including the impact of inverter characteristics on the frequency-voltage relationship, which defines the maximum allowable power imbalance. By applying Lyapunov theory, we derive a potential function to create feasible guidelines for ensuring stability.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are increasingly evolving into intelligent entities capable of adapting to shifting environments, which has given rise to Cyber-physical Systems of Systems (CPSoS) aimed at optimizing overall performance. This dissertation investigates the empowerment required for individual CPS within a CPSoS hierarchy to function effectively. Through a thorough analysis of an exemplary CPS, the author delineates the necessary intelligence capabilities and proposes a conceptual framework for these interactions. The work presents intelligence not as a standalone attribute but as a dynamic interplay between capability and function, ensuring that each CPS contributes meaningfully to systemic goals. The proposed architecture is validated through the analysis and design processes of an unstructured CPS example, demonstrating its efficacy in achieving system-wide objectives.

Certain blazers display an ultraviolet (UV) and/or soft X-ray excess in their spectra, a feature often interpreted as evidence for photon beaming effects within a relativistically rotating or precessing jet. To rigorously evaluate this hypothesis, a Monte Carlo simulation called MAPPIES was developed to account for complex scenarios that exceed the explanatory limits of simple models involving a power-law distribution under relativistic inversion Compton (IC) scattering. Specifically, MAPPIES incorporates variations in electron kinetic, a double-thermal electron population structure, and radiation from diverse sources such as external fields, internal synchrotron emission, and radiation reflected by jet components, all within a relativistically transforming frame. Applying this methodology to the blazar PKS 1622-297, this study finds that the observed UV and soft X-ray excess can indeed arise from multiple Compton scattering of synchrotron photons by a sub-thermally distributed electron population. Furthermore, multiple Compton emission is established as a critical, albeit often overlooked, component in modeling the broad-band spectra of this astronomical sources class.

The analysis indicates that string fragmentation yields primarily three-quark states (baryons) alongside four-quark states (tetrabaryons). The resulting mass spectrum displays oscillations characteristic of star-like string configurations, resembling the oscillations seen in linear strings. Notably, the model predicts the lightest tetrabaryon mass to be approximately the same as that of a standard three-quark baryon. Furthermore, the mass spectrum for heavy flavor baryons exhibits significant splitting, a result of spin-orbit interactions. The alignment of these generated baryon and meson spectra with experimental data is notably strong. In contrast to linear strings, the quantized fragmentation of helical strings produces fragments with significantly lower mass.

The growing demand for precise and extensive spatial data has prompted numerous countries to adopt and refine area-level estimation and direct survey collection strategies. The authors propose a streamlined model for Direct Small Area Estimation (D-SAE) that incorporates auxiliary data and spatial correlation, offering substantial computational and sampling efficiency. Utilizing simulations, this study compares the performance of such frameworks, specifically in terms of bias, mean squared error, and overall operational efficiency, and utilizes a dataset from South Africa to inform its design. The research demonstrates that spatial models can enhance the accuracy of Direct Small Area Estimation, particularly when applied to post-stratified estimates for small or intermediate population groups. Furthermore, it is observed that spatial models yield greater efficiency when the structure of the auxiliary variables is accurately specified. However, this study also reveals that non-spatial post-stratification remains highly effective and warrants continued use in D-SAE, especially for very small population groups.

This investigation explores the optimal strategy for betting on the outcomes of single radioactive decay events using a continuous-variable quantum representation. The primary objective is to establish a fully real domain optimal Kelly betting formula. Leveraging a quantum parameterized approach for the payoff model—specifically through the introduction of an imaginary parameter within the Hilbert space—we derive closed-form solutions for the optimum betting factor, valid across any and all possible decay results. This formulation is subsequently applied to interpret data regarding single neutron mass measurements.

We conducted first-principles calculations to determine the band alignment of the two-layer $\text{MA}_2\text{Z}_4$ ($\text{M} = \text{Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; Z = N, P, \text{or As}$) monolayer materials, specifically investigating the $\text{AA'}$ and $\text{AB}$ stacking configurations. The results reveal that the alignment type is not solely dictated by chemical composition but is also influenced by stacking order. In both configurations, the valence band maximum (VBM) originates from the p orbitals of atom A, whereas the conduction band minimum (CBM) arises from the p orbitals of atom M. Notably, in the $\text{AA'}$ arrangement, the CBM is located at the $\Gamma$ point, while for the $\text{AB}$ configuration, the minimum occurs at the K point. Additionally, the exciton binding energy remains consistently high across all studied systems, typically ranging from $0.2$ to $0.4$ eV, and shows minimal sensitivity to the employed stacking method.

The formation and subsequent evolution of planets rely fundamentally on disk formation, which naturally arises from the collapse of molecular cloud cores. Despite this established mechanism, observed planet-forming disks are significantly more turbulent than the minimal rotation required by simple models of core implosion, suggesting that the standard scenario lacks critical details. Utilizing the high-resolution GADGET-3 code, this study examines the structure and dynamics of young disks within a realistic star-forming environment. It specifically focuses on a massive core located in the Ophiuchus cluster, which accretes from a surrounding, highly turbulent and rotating gas envelope. The simulation demonstrates that interactions between this turbulent and rotating nebular gas and the forming core generate a massive, dynamic, and turbulent disk. Furthermore, mass accretion from the envelope causes the disk to shift toward rotation-dominated behavior, creating a distinct phase of turbulence that contradicts observations of isolated disks in quiescent clouds. It is argued that this turbulent accretion phase, rather than a stationary turbulent configuration, characterizes many young stars in clusters, offering a comprehensive framework for disk creation and a vital step toward understanding planet formation.

Atmospheric dispersion is a pivotal factor in high-precision astronomical observations, a fact particularly true for those targeting narrow line-of-sight features. While numerous instruments and adaptive optics systems incorporate on-sky characterization of this phenomenon, the comprehensive and quantitative link between observed on-sky measurements and model predictions remains underexplored. This research quantifies the discrepancies between model-based expectations and actual observations across various conditions, specifically examining how atmospheric properties in the measurements align with models. We demonstrate that this approach enables the direct determination of key atmospheric parameters from observational data. Notably, the study reveals a strong correlation between the dispersion produced on-sky and specific characterizations of the atmosphere, providing direct measurement of this link through observational data.

This study addresses the challenge of predicting time series data across several consecutive periods. We propose a new deep learning architecture featuring a convolutional initial layer to capture local temporal patterns and a subsequent recurrent layer to model dependencies across periods. Additionally, we implement a inference method using the variational approach, integrated with sparsity constraints and a prior distribution, to enable the variable selection of specific periods. The result is a more refined and streamlined deep learning framework designed for multi-period prediction. Empirical comparisons on synthetic data and real-world financial records demonstrate that our method achieves superior forecasting accuracy and correctly identifies the most relevant periods for prediction.

The significant achievements driven by deep learning have introduced numerous challenges to machine learning practitioners, particularly regarding fairness in prediction and the confidentiality of data. Moreover, we highlight the interactions among model efficacy, fairness, and privacy, and conclude by outlining potential future research avenues within this domain.

The theory also incorporates a right-handed chiral superfield, $\chi$, charged under $U(1)_X$, which functions as a singlet in the Standard Model. The Majorana fermion derived from $\chi$ is proposed as a dark matter candidate. The model's viability hinges on determining a $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling that remains perturbative up to the Planck scale, a condition that can be satisfied by adjusting the Yukawa coupling associated with $\chi$. The $\omega$ mass spectrum is highly sensitive to this specific $U(1)_X$ gauge coupling, resulting in a broad spectrum that aligns with dark matter constraints. Furthermore, radiative electroweak symmetry breaking is observed, suggesting that this framework offers an attractive avenue for investigating supersymmetric dark matter candidates operating at the TeV scale.

Unlike universal pixel-based attacks, UGDL exploits the features of quantum neural networks to create adversarial examples that induce quantum classifiers to output incorrect results with maximum confidence, effectively bypassing the need for a theoretical framework. Unlike other universal attack strategies, it does not rely on the specific geometry of the quantum decision boundary. Instead, it employs gradient ascent to optimize the objective function, demonstrating the creation of robustness against various quantum models, including those based on parameterized quantum circuits and the Variational Quantum EigenSolver. This technique achieves significant performance gains, reducing classification error rates to near-zero levels.

Conformance checking focuses on reconciling recorded behavior derived from system runs with their corresponding process models. Alignments represent this checking mechanism on a bit-level scale, where they combine the features of system executions and specific traversal paths within the process model to calculate the distance between the two. Existing algorithms primarily depend on infix alignments to perform this calculation. This thesis proposes a new algorithm capable of generating infix alignments efficiently. It has been demonstrated that this method is effective not only at producing such alignments but is also fully compatible with the scoring mechanisms found in standard conformance checking protocols. The research further explores the integration of postfix alignments—a variation differing only in the reordering rules of mismatch calculations—within these algorithms. The outcome of this study is a performance-improved algorithm that generates postfix alignments using the same logic. Additionally, I have established that these algorithms are sound with regard to their delivery of such alignments. The practical utility of this approach is illustrated by comparing how different scoring methods perform and by detailing their specific applications.

This study introduces a new neural network framework for modeling cellular network radio propagation, designed to learn mapping from imagery to propagation parameters. The proposed architecture relies on a three-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) that integrates network topology maps, satellite imagery, and satellite-derived geophysical data. We evaluate the framework using satellite data covering 500,000 square kilometers in the continental United States, parameterized via Large-Scale Site-to-Site (S2S) measurements. Within a cellular planning context where precise propagation models are essential, our approach offers a high-fidelity alternative to conventional methods like the ITM, COST231, or Small-Scale Site-to-Site models, thereby enhancing network optimization, planning, and planning efficiency.

Our evaluation demonstrates two primary findings. First, the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, including the ITM, COST231, and Small-Scale configurations. Second, it exhibits superior scalability when processing networks characterized by high density and vast geographic extents compared to traditional methodologies.

This paper presents a formal semantics framework and a formally verified validation algorithm for Temporal Planning, a subclass of PDDL2.1 PDDL which incorporates time-controlling features. We define Temporal Planning as a decision process to find solutions for problems that meet time and resource constraints. Although this validation algorithm is practical and used in real-world applications, it conflicts with standard practices; the root cause of this issue is the absence of a shared understanding of the algorithm's behavior. Our contribution establishes a rigorous mathematical definition of this behavior. First, we propose a new formulation of Temporal Planning problems. Second, we propose to model the problem's natural language description using description logics to guide the development of the validation algorithm. Our proposed solution involves a algorithm that leverages the EL knowledge representation language and satisfies quadratic computational complexity. Our main achievement involves formally verifying the algorithm's correctness and ensuring the consistency between the original paper's description and our implementation using Leonardo, a specialized theorem prover for linguistics applications.

Optimization-based power system expansion plans are typically sensitive to data inputs such as costs, load projections, and generation costs; however, this study examines a distinct aspect: the variability of these models regarding system constraints and the assumed planning horizon. Using a case study based on the Northwest of France, this research assesses how model outputs shift when different constraints are applied and when the planning horizon is either short-term (5 years) or long-term (20 years). Specifically, we compare a long-term expansion model that includes network capacity constraints against a short-term counterpart that excludes them. The primary objective is to highlight the principal generation and infrastructure differences that arise from varying these parameters, demonstrating that the choice of both constraints and time horizons holds major implications for the resulting power system expansion outcomes.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for various Vlasov-Poisson-type systems under bounded boundary constraints. By representing the electric field as a series expansion involving spherical harmonic moments of density fluctuations around the mean value, we derive a corresponding system of coupled nonlinear partial differential equations. The proof of the well-posedness of this derived system to all times relies on an energy estimate method supplemented by careful analytical bounds on the coefficients linked to domain geometry. Ultimately, our explicit solutions demonstrate that the derived higher-order partial system adequately captures the essential physical characteristics of the original Vlasov-Poisson framework.

Software maintenance heavily relies on conceptual understanding, where concepts represent meaningful entities like classes, methods, or fields within the source code. While existing literature extensively explores concept localization techniques, current tools frequently rely on flawed or inconsistent metadata, resulting in inadequate precision. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages advanced software engineering (SE) data to automatically derive search queries directly from maintenance tasks (e.g., GitHub Issues). Using STRICT (Search Term Identification for Concept Concept Localization), the system integrates various SE artifacts to pinpoint relevant code elements corresponding to specific concepts defined in issues. The methodology was evaluated across a comprehensive dataset comprising issues from 17 leading open-source projects. The results indicate that, on average, the proposed approach successfully identified the correct location for approximately 64% of these concepts, implying that STRICT could effectively aid maintainers in accurately grasping task-related requirements and reducing errors upon implementation.

Colloidal gels possess both a solid-like structure at rest and fluid-like consistency under shear, making them ideal candidates for "rheo-acoustic" manipulation, where their rheological properties are tuned using ultrasonic waves. In this study, we demonstrate the controlled adjustment of rheological characteristics within an acoustically responsive, weakly polydisperse colloidal gel using two distinct surfaces: flat ones and patterned ones featuring microscale cavities. Flat regions maintain a thick gel state even during acoustic manipulation, whereas gel thinning occurs exclusively over patterned areas under acoustic exposure. Surface patterns emerge solely within these open zones, allowing gel viscosity and elastic modulus to shift from their initial values by more than two orders of magnitude in both scenarios. High-speed video analysis reveals that surface patterns thicken into gels due to acoustic-induced gelation, while flat regions thin into sols through dehydration and particle alignment facilitated by the waves. Pattern-based gels exhibit a viscoelastic response driven by frequency-dependent acoustic forces, while those on flat surfaces show a time-dependent drop in elastic modulus as dehydration advances. These findings establish a pathway for creating advanced surface-engineered ultrasonic transducers capable of precisely controlling fluid dynamics within microfluidic systems.

This work addresses the conjecture regarding infinite sequences of odd numbers, derived from applying a specific arithmetic rule to supply integers; the sequence exhibits a pattern of growth and contraction, though the theorem remains unproven to date.

Classifying documents by subject is vital for organizing (digital) libraries and enabling data-driven research. While text-based approaches are common, this work proposes a new method for clustering STEM documents by integrating existing knowledge of mathematical notation. We achieve this by utilizing a model of math notation that enables us to maintain the full knowledge of such symbols for downstream applications. We use an entity-linking model to explain the importance of linking these symbols to a standardized bank of 10,688 mathematical definitions. Experiments demonstrate that incorporating these linked items in a multi-label setting significantly enhances document clustering by incorporating the full value and meaning of 10,688 linked items.

This paper addresses an expanded version of the classic distributed, stable marriage problem. We consider agents who are initially unaware of the entire set of all possible proposals. The only guiding principle for these agents is their preference for a proposal over the default option of remaining unmatched. These agents may either favor the possibility of making additional unsolicited offerings or opt to simply submit their initial set of suggestions. The primary objective is to design strategies that collectively result in a matching with the highest overall social utility. We demonstrate the optimal approach for a single, isolated agent but reveal a complication when multiple agents are present: the lack of information regarding the rival strategies can render the best choice ambiguous. To resolve this, we evaluate whether a prior consensus on the optimal strategy is necessary or if a robust mechanism exists to guarantee a strong outcome regardless of how other agents behave. The analysis concludes by pinpointing the precise agent types for whom an obligation to disclose the strategy beforehand is essential versus those who can confidently proceed without it.

Summary evaluation metrics are essential for summarization model development and, ultimately, their performance assessment. However, existing metrics often fail to accurately gauge summary quality, mainly because they calculate similarity against original documents in ways inherent model biases and input encodings introduce. This paper introduces SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation model designed to overcome these limitations. Unlike traditional metrics that merely average pairwise similarities between a candidate summary and multiple summaries in the gold set, SummScore employs cross-encoding to model candidate-gold interactions more effectively by leveraging rich semantic features learned from training data. This innovative model significantly boosts accuracy in summary quality evaluation by integrating advanced cross-encoding capabilities with dynamic, context-aware representations derived from both candidate and reference parallel word embeddings in memory banks. Comprehensive experiments confirm that SumScorc achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple standard benchmarks. Furthermore, sumscore demonstrates robustness against domain shifts when compared to existing metrics which struggle in such scenarios.

This paper focuses on recovering an unknown, sparse vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ from compressed observations of the form $\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^2 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n}$. Here, $\boldsymbol{\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ represents a random matrix with independent rows, while $\mathbf{n}$ denotes a vector of Gaussian noise. The study investigates the theoretical limits of recovery in the sparse regime and proposes a new estimator based on maximum-likelihood principles. This method requires solving a convex optimization problem by representing $\mathbf{x}$ as a non-negative linear combination of the canonical basis vectors. The authors derive a bound for the mean-squared error of the proposed estimator and demonstrate that, provided the number of measurements $m$ scales as $\mathcal{O}(n/K \log(n))$ where $K$ is the sparsity level, the error remains bounded below by a constant times $n$. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical experiments and are compared against the performance of the Gross's Lasso.

Integrating camera and LiDAR data is vital for many autonomous driving applications. Although existing frameworks are abundant, they typically require specific sensor fusion strategies for distinct tasks and often fail to fully utilize data from both modalities. While recent methods attempt joint utilization, they usually rely on heuristic approaches that are sensitive to data distribution shifts and to the quality of LiDAR-cameras synchronization. To address these gaps, we present BEVFusion, a straightforward yet powerful framework for fusing LiDAR and camera inputs. This approach leverages the unified 3D vehicle coordinate representation generated by BEVFusion to simplify fusion logic into two key stages: (1) deriving cross-modal attention weights via cross-entropy in the unified space, and (2) aggregating cross-attended BEVFacts to enhance representations. Our experiments indicate that BEVFusion surpasses current state-of-the-art frameworks, demonstrating robustness against various synchronization errors. Furthermore, this framework is highly extensible to support diverse downstream tasks.

While conventional wisdom holds that thermal agitation influences hydrodynamics only within the infrared-to-visible spectrum, our current model demonstrates that the solid's temperature also dictates the magnitude of these fluctuations at the source. Consequently, as the thermal amplitude rises, they intensify dissipation through enhanced random fluid motion, ultimately superimposing a state of turbulent equilibrium characterized by saturated velocity variations against the background of turbulent flow. Our analysis examines interactions between bare fluids and thermal excitations in paramagnetic salts during both low temperature regimes and high temperature regimes, exploring the combined effects of bare fluid activity and thermal agitation throughout various spatial and temporal scales. This study presents H-STREAM, a machine learning pipeline designed to facilitate both real-time and delayed analysis of massive data streams and historical datasets. It introduces a universal interface for stream processing, data stream management, relational stream management, and parallel computation, which serves as the backbone of H-STREAM. This engine was benchmarked against leading systems, including DB2 LMDS and DB2 LMDS, demonstrating that H-STREAM is significantly faster than those systems. The research also outlines how H-STREAM can be utilized to solve practical problems within the domain of computer vision, specifically pedestrian and vehicle detection, highlighting its effectiveness in processing high-resolution video streams. The system was tested on the well-known PASCAL VOC 2011 and COCO 2011 datasets, which are widely regarded as the gold standards in the field. The results indicate that H-STREAM outperforms the baseline system by over 100%, making it highly suitable for a variety of applications. The source code is available at: https://github.com/IBM/hstream.

Investigating supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking mechanisms motivates the investigation of heavy partners linked to Standard Model (SM) fermions, specifically top and bottom partners. When produced at a hadron collider, cross-sections for Standard production processes are generally suppressed and insufficient for securing a robust discovery; however, techniques to enhance these standard cross-sections are essential. This study focuses on non-resonant single production channels for both top and bottom partners that arise from weak boson or Higgs boson exchange, alongside associated SM fermion pair production. We analyze the interplay between these non-resonant contributions and other reaction channels and determine their capability to boost total cross-sections. Furthermore, we present anticipated signal yields for various production mechanisms that could be observed in $14~\mathrm{TeV}$ proton-proton collisions, assuming a coupling to the SM top or bottom quark that deviates from the naive minimal supergravity (NMSSM) framework.

Knowledge-Base-Base grounded conversational systems are increasingly prevalent across numerous real-world applications. As dialogue progresses, dialogue state tracking (DST) is essential to record user information provided during conversation. Dialogue elements are often stored and accessed using logic formalisms like SPARQL queries derived from a knowledge base (KB). However, neural dialogue state tracking models face difficulties in processing these elements because standard architectures like attention or Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) struggle to replicate exact textual copies from the input to the output. To resolve this, we suggest a new dual-directional copy mechanism that effectively captures and reproduces these components. Our proposed system is integrated into the existing Dual-Attention Gated Recurrent network (DGRU). Empirical results demonstrate that this copy mechanism significantly boosts DGRU's efficacy in handling KB components.

Scholarly research relies heavily on venues—journals, conferences, and repositories—as their primary organizational units. Analyzing venues offers a straightforward method to evaluate research quality and discover trends within specific fields of study. However, the current primary metric, citation count, is flawed; it fails to reflect a venue's actual impact, creates strong positive feedback loops that favor established institutions, and lacks neutrality.

We propose a new methodology, Venue Analytics, designed to provide comprehensive insights into research locations. Our primary innovation is the development of a distinct quality metric grounded in network science, which effectively complements traditional data. We demonstrate the utility and breadth of this approach by performing broad-stroke analyses across 1,055 computer science venues, as well as targeted examinations of 26 top conferences in various sub-disciplines.

The comprehensive Venue Analytics report integrates multiple dimensions, including research production, quality, and influence, while also examining the temporal evolution of these factors. We further investigate the dynamics of "venue switching," where scholars publish in one venue and subsequently in another, to map the dynamic relationships between research hubs. Additionally, we analyze "citationsphere" networks to chart how researchers converge on specific venues through mutual citation patterns.

Neural networks have become a significant innovation in control systems, yet their verifiability remains a primary concern for users. To address this, the paper reviews existing neural network verification techniques within the control domain, highlighting the theoretical strengths and limitations of each approach based on their inherent characteristics.

Tensor completion techniques are widely used for recovering large-scale tensor data with extensive missing entries. Unlike methods that process entire tensors at once, a novel framework utilizing tensor ring completion to track streaming patches from a large collection of images offers distinct advantages. This approach not only achieves superior recovery performance but also demands substantially lower computational memory compared to global completion strategies. Furthermore, this paper introduces a streamable, patch-tracking-based algorithm that iterates through patches either in random order or sorted by their similarity to previously seen data. Empirical results demonstrate that this patch-tracking method outperforms general tensor ring completion and various state-of-the-art techniques. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining the ability to process visual data sequentially with minimal memory footprint.

We investigate graded Nichols algebras of degree one arising from finite reflections in both characteristic zero and positive characteristic settings. Our primary achievement provides explicit computations of the degree of the Poincaré series for both cases, demonstrating that it corresponds to the order of the Weyl group acting on the associated reflections in each characteristic setting.

This study employs numerical simulations to investigate turbulence within rotating stratified fluids, specifically analyzing the energy spectrum for inertial waves characterized by a fixed angle relative to the vertical axis. Surprisingly, a broad class of non-circularly-polarized wave modes simultaneously exhibits a consistent spectral slope. We provide an analytical proof for this specific slope by demonstrating that vector wave number modes can be decomposed into pairs of helical modes with opposing rotation but matching wavenumber magnitudes. Furthermore, this study compares computational outcomes with the standard model of Langmuir wave turbulence to determine if they align. The results indicate a significant parallelism between inertial wave turbulence and Langmuir wave turbulence.

This work examines two algorithms: the first iteratively normalizes weights on a graph, while the second constructs a graph-driven model of maximal weights and independent sets. The study establishes a polynomial-time verifiable necessary condition for the exactness of the second algorithm and provides a tight upper bound for its error when this condition is violated. Additionally, it introduces a threshold condition that acts as an interval for a specific graph weight feature; the second algorithm exhibits constant accuracy within this range and behaves errorlessly if and only that the weight falls outside the range. Finally, it characterizes two graph classes where the algorithm performs either perfectly or consistently with constant accuracy.

This study investigates the electrical tuning of thermodynamic and electronic properties in single-layer graphene by applying an external periodic electrostatic potential along the armchair edge. Results indicate that applying a longitudinal periodic electrostatic potential suppresses the charge density in those regions. The density response closely follows the applied potential, and a higher potential magnitude leads to a more significant charge depletion. Utilizing the density response function derived from the MRPA approach, the energy response is calculated and analyzed in the MD-landau random phase framework. This study employs low-frequency observations from the Lofar Low-Frequency Array to investigate the long-term evolution of the electron-cyclotron maser (EM) emission associated with the binary system CD Dra. During a 12-day observation window in 2019, Lofar detected intense bursts of radio bursts ranging from 100 to 200 MHz, occurring just before the system's more massive star completed nearly one full orbit. These bursts recur daily throughout the observation period, synchronizing precisely with each stellar orbit. However, this duality—daily orbital periodicity and a longer-term cycle—indicates two distinct periods of variability. While the short-term fluctuations correlate with the primary star's orbit, the long-term pattern aligns with the orbit of the second star, which is a young, active M dwarf. This behavior confirms that the radio bursts originate from the planetary mass companion (a hot Jupiter-like exoplanet) orbiting the flare star CD Dra, specifically as a young, active star influences the system.
