Creating photorealistic animations and interactions for virtual humans is a critical requirement across numerous sectors, yet simulating realistic skin reflections and subsurface scattering remains difficult because modeling these optical behaviors alongside consistent 3D human shapes requires extensive, annotated training datasets. Although current techniques that leverage motion capture data can produce realistic animations with real human textures, they fail to account for the influence of body mechanics on light interaction, resulting in visually unconvincing outcomes. This paper introduces Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a system capable of simulating physically accurate 3D human skin while tracking articulated motion. Our approach utilizes motion capture data to parametrically represent human poses and learn to predict these poses along with corresponding global lighting conditions from real video recordings. A generative adversarial neural rendering framework is then trained to predict a fixed set of skin rendering parameters that accurately reproduce an user's skin characteristics across various viewpoints, varying expressions, and motion capture sequences. The separation between shared lighting/pose variability and consistent individual skin properties allows ANR to generate high-fidelity virtual avatars from standard capture sessions. Experimental results across diverse scenarios—such as self-portraits, selfies, and self-illuminated environments—demonstrate that ARN produces significantly more realistic imagery than existing methods.

While recent advancements in computer vision have yielded impressive results, humans remain the ultimate standard for assessment; thus, aligning machine predictions with human perception is essential. However, significant differences in how humans and machines react to extreme visual manipulations, such as color inversion, have been identified. This study presents a specialized benchmark featuring highly transformed images to evaluate the convergence of human and machine performance. Notably, even after implementing corrections, machines differ fundamentally from humans, who effectively disregard extreme transformations during evaluation, a skill not yet replicated by algorithms despite various attempts to match this ability by reducing the gap in accuracy.

This study investigates the emergence of the Askey-Wilson (AW) algebra within the context of Wilson loop expectation values represented by Brafim's state model in the $SU(2)$ Chern-Simons theory at level $k$. This analysis focuses on Brafim's basis states corresponding to braided eigenstates of the R-matrix acting on Wilson line configurations where the lines meet at a single point, with intersection multiplicity of three for pairs of lines. It is demonstrated that the Brafim's basis states associated with a tetrahedral arrangement of lines obey operator relations governed by a set of generators satisfying the structural properties defined by a universal Askey-Wilson algebra. Consequently, the generators of this AW algebra act as operators on the state space of the system, and it is established that the algebra of these operators is universally isomorphic to a specific concrete isomorphism of the AW algebra. This framework establishes a mechanism for deriving new properties concerning the representation of the AW algebra and provides the means to construct specific representations of the algebra, notably a faithful representation. As a significant outcome, this result facilitates the demonstration of the conjectured universal isomorphism of the AW algebra of the infinite rank variety proposed by Caenepeel and Van de Voort. This conclusion holds for an infinite family of Askey-Wilson algebras defined by Bira and de Voort.

This paper reports mean-field phase diagrams for two classes of two-dimensional network antiferromagnerts featuring weakly linked frustrated trimers: the network derived from the $CaCu_2O_4$ structure and the $Na_2Cu_3O_{2-p}O'_2$ structure. Utilizing cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations, the study reveals that low-temperature behavior in both systems is well-explained by the ground states of weakly coupled trimer units, where each unit exhibits exclusively frustrated triangular motifs. Despite the full system lacking global long-range order, the substructures of the trimers do support it. We focus on the short-range order dynamics of these trimer components, analyzing how they evolve as interaction strengths between them vary. The findings align with prior findings from other methods regarding the weak-field limit of these trimer bond states and highlight the limitations of applying extended cluster extensions to highly frustrated networks.

Large-scale pre-trained models, such as GPT-3, have shown promising results when employed for zero-shot learning (ZSL). However, it has been observed that the optimal zero-shot solution varies depending on the specific target task. To the best of our knowledge, no study has yet explored the automatic adaptation of these language models for individual ZSL problems by identifying and combining similar tasks. In this work, we present a novel approach that generalizes from related natural language processing (NLP) tasks to effectively transfer knowledge to previously unseen zero-shot problems. We introduce a large-scale repository of open-source datasets and problems for Natural Language Understanding (NLU) and Natural Language Generation (NLG). We also introduce a new meta-tuning strategy, which involves training a single model on a sequence of these tasks. Tackering the challenge of varying input formats across different datasets, we develop a unifying approach for processing diverse NLU and NLG data. We then train the model on the entire collection of problems and demonstrate that it can be quickly and effectively fine-tuned for any of the zero-shot tasks covered in training. The results reveal that pre-trained models, such as RoBERTa and T5, achieve state-of-the-art performance across the board when the model is fine-tuned on a single zero-shot issue, but also show that our method can be used to select the best subset of zero-shot problems for fine-tuning to achieve top-tier results across the entire NLU-NLG spectrum

We examine the potential of G. W. E. O. (GW. E. O. Gravitational Waves Observ) to detect gravitational waves arising from a strong first-order electroweak phase transition in the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model extended with a $Z_3$ symmetry (NMSSM with $Z_3$-invariance). Our analysis incorporates the latest LHC Run 2 constraints, including the LHCb's latest findings on the dark photon search, as well as direct dark matter search results like those from XENON1T and LUX-ZEPLIN. We demonstrate that the theory can simultaneously satisfy all existing experimental constraints while simultaneously producing a strong enough electroweak phase transition to generate a significant gravitational wave signal detectable by LIGO-Virgo.

Redshift measurement constitutes a fundamental task for the next generation of cosmological surveys. This study introduces a statistical diagnostic tool designed to evaluate the robustness of redshift estimation methods. Its approach relies on comparing two metrics derived from observed data: the distribution of inferred estimates and the distribution of true input values. We term the histogram of inferred redshifts the \textit{prior} distribution and the distribution of supplied truth values the \textit{likelihood} distribution. The primary objective is to align these two distributions, a comparison we quantify using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. This methodology has been validated using simulations from the High-z Sudoku project—a Bayesian Bayesian machine learning pipeline for inferring redshifts from cosmological line emission spectra—and is also applicable to other algorithms. The tool effectively identified that High-z Sudoku delivers unbiased and statistically consistent redshifts, with a precision of $\sigma_z \approx 0.02$ across the universe ($z \sim 1-5$ range). Conversely, the analysis revealed that a Markov Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian method, which models spectra as a sum of Gaussians, produces significantly biased results under the same conditions.

We investigate the dynamical properties of a finite-temperature, finite-size Heisenberg antiferromagnet situated on a triangular lattice through the lens of matrix product states (MPS) and thermodynamic limit extrapolation. Specifically, we analyze both static and dynamical correlation functions. A key requirement for next-generation atomic sensors is the development of miniaturized, high-density vapor cells. This approach utilizes the device's integrated silicon structure as a transparent window, eliminating the need for traditional, optically lossy materials like quartz or sapphire. These high-density cells, which incorporate the sophisticated "lens-in-lens" geometry, are capable of holding up to 400 Rb pressure and are suitable for integration into high-performance atomics devices, including near-field atomic force microscopy sensors and magnetometers.

Network science offers a powerful framework for examining complex systems through their fundamental components and the intricate connections binding them together. This discipline leverages diverse methods to analyze network characteristics, with key techniques including various centrality measures, which quantify a node's relative importance within a structure. The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics (EED), characterized by the rapid interplay of ecological and evolutionary changes, is currently a vibrant domain. This interest stems from its ability to address fundamental biological questions, enhance the management of complex living systems, and improve critical practical applications such as pandemic control and cancer therapies. Nevertheless, a significant disconnect persists between traditional concepts rooted in deep-time evolution and modern, contemporary dynamics. Consequently, a unified theoretical framework remains elusive, hindering both mathematical modeling and empirical advancements. This gap is largely driven by a lack of systematic identification and testing of key variables that govern these interactions. This article synthesizes existing knowledge to examine how the speed and direction of evolution influence ecological and evolutionary processes. High-energy X-ray and ultraviolet (UV) radiation from stellar activity can erode planetary atmospheres and degrade organic molecules, posing a significant constraint on habitability within the habitable zone. We report the first observations of EUV flux from the active M-dwarf AU Mic during both quiescent and flaring periods, utilizing data from the 2014-2015 mission of the Hinode satellite. To our knowledge, this marks the initial detection of a single flare from a single star across the full range of wavelengths from 1 nm to 800 nm. We modeled quiescent spectra using the, and flaring spectra using, to derive the stellar emission measure as the flare progressed. Our analysis of AU Mic's quiescent FUV spectrum suggests that the previously estimated habitable zone edge—calculated based on Earth-like atmospheric retention limits—is over 40\% too distant from the star, and that the orbiting planets AU Mic b (a super-Earth) and Au Mic c (a sub-Neptune) likely experience atmospheric loss rates of $10$ to $10$ per year. Reactions to radiation have long been acknowledged as causing energy loss by accelerating particles. While this phenomenon is well-documented, its connection to a material medium with resistance remains unclear. We aim to clarify this relationship and establish a theoretical framework that effectively integrates material resistivity into the model of radiative damping. Our analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, radiative friction can surpass the traditional drag force generated by collisions. Additionally, we explore outcomes such as the deceleration of objects moving at constant speed and the periodic oscillatory motion of radiation-driven systems.

In recent years, nearest neighbor classification has become increasingly popular for analyzing large datasets. However, many practical datasets are inherently imbalanced, rendering conventional nearest neighbor methods ineffective because they prioritize majority classes rather than minority classes. To address this limitation, our work evaluates several techniques designed to handle imbalance within nearest neighbor classification. Specifically, we compare these methods using both synthetic datasets and real-world data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, with all outcomes assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Furthermore, we also examine how varying parameter settings in our proposed methods influence their classification performance.

We have identified 22 new ultra-luminous optically-selected quasars at redshifts $6.5 < z < 9.0$ using SkyMapper, with absolute magnitudes ranging from $-18.0 < M_B < -29.0$ and observed fluxes between $1.0 < F_B < 10.0$ mJy. These new discoveries, combined with 14 previously reported ultra-luminous quasars, were used to construct the bright end of the ultra-luminous quasar luminosity function (ULLLF). The analysis reveals a power-law distribution, $ \phi(\ge M_B) \propto -0.84 \pm 0.13 $. Additionally, we find that the number density of the most luminous quasars at $z=9$ is $1.2^{+1.1}_{-0.7} \times 10^{-10} \, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3} \, \mathrm{mag}^{-1}$ for $M_B > -29.0$ (assuming a standard cosmological model).

This framework encompasses boundary equilibrium solutions for numerous physical models, including water waves, isentropic and non-isentropic gas dynamics, and magneto-hydrodynamics. The challenge of creating indefinite novel viewpoints through virtual forward motion in multi-view photography is referred to as Perpetual View Generation. A prevalent approach utilizes a trained model to synthesize these scenes based on a provided single-image prompt. However, existing methods struggle with maintaining texture fidelity and often produce geometric distortions, particularly in the areas distant from the input view. To address this limitation, we introduce DiffDreamer, an innovative framework leveraging conditional diffusion for high-quality perpetual view generation from single static images. Unlike previous models that merely append depth information to the condition without fully leveraging it, our strategy employs a guided depth diffusion mechanism to produce geometrically consistent outputs while simultaneously refining texture via a multi-view alignment loss during inference. Furthermore, our model effectively preserves long-term geometric consistency across extended generation sequences by leveraging autoregressive generation and aligning overlapping fields of view within the depth maps. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that DiffDreamer significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques on both synthetic and real-world data.

Complex systems, like those depicted by networked processes, rely on intricate interactions between components, making it difficult to quantify how these connections influence system behavior. While graph theory is often used to map these interactions, the resulting difficulty in deriving a closed-form dynamic model frequently hampers effective decision-making. Nevertheless, specific characteristics of such systems, such as their graph topology, can be exploited to facilitate model learning. This work presents a framework leveraging this approach for networked systems to enhance both prediction and optimization. It begins by proposing the use of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to identify the interactions within the target process. Subsequently, an algorithm is developed to optimize these systems under constraints, where a key advantage lies in their independence from any prior knowledge regarding the underlying dynamics. The proposed methods are validated through an analysis of the networked Susceptible-Infected susceptible (SIS) model, demonstrating that the framework successfully infers both the process and its interaction structure. Furthermore, simulations indicate that the learned model supports high-accuracy prediction and optimization outcomes.

This study introduces a novel methodology for duration modeling in speech synthesis that relies on the medians of duration distributions. In contrast to the standard HMM framework that estimates models from mean values, our approach utilizes median data, allowing speech segments to maintain their original temporal lengths during speech unit decoding. This inherent retention of temporal data obviates the need for separate models for duration prediction, as the statistical significance (medians) is directly derived. Furthermore, the application of robust statistical measures like the median mitigates distortion caused by outliers, as such values have minimal impact on the resulting model parameters and training dynamics. In addition, the proposal features a non-parametric generation technique for synthetic duration corpora. Synthetic files are produced by randomly shuffling phoneme sequences from existing speech data, maintaining phoneme-level durations while adjusting them according to the statistical distributions (medians) learned from specific speaker diarization data. The speech quality of this synthesized data is validated through comparison with the source recordings using Automatic Speech Recognition metrics.

Identifying hate speech on social media platforms is increasingly critical given the vast volume of data generated. Our work introduces a method to detect hate speech by leveraging a feature extraction approach that employs a transformer-based BERT model. To the best of our knowledge, this specific implementation using BERT has not been previously explored for this purpose, and the results achieved by our approach are highly competitive. Specifically, on the HassIsHere dataset, this method reaches an F1 score of 0.9129 on the test set, surpassing all existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, on the ISIS-Ar dataset with its balanced evaluation metrics, it attains a score of 0.8649, where it ranks as the second-best performer.

This study introduces novel feature-sharing strategies for Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) networks designed to enhance both computational efficiency and performance. By leveraging bidirectional connections and applying the feature-sharing technique, these networks automatically create a shared representation that integrates both local and global characteristics. These improvements significantly reduce the number of parameters and the cost of forward and backward passes. The model achieves a state-of-the-art performance with 31.8% fewer parameters and 31.8% less computational effort compared to existing Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) benchmarks. Additionally, the new architecture uses only 57.3% of the parameters and 51.87% of the computational effort relative to comparable Multi-Input Multi-Output Convolutional Neural Network (MICO CNN) approaches.

This survey offers a comprehensive overview of 25 public, open-access datasets specializing in historical document image processing. We provide a detailed description of dataset characteristics and categorize them by image format, content origin, annotation type, and specific domain. For each dataset, a summary of published processing pipelines—including those for correction, segmentation, and recognition—is also included. The article aims to assist researchers in selecting appropriate datasets for image correction, segmentation, and recognition tasks. It seeks to facilitate the development of digitization infrastructure for cultural institutions and to develop automated systems for processing historical documents across various domains and eras.

Achieving high-precision trajectory tracking remains a significant challenge for industrial robots equipped with standard reducers and motors, a limitation often caused by transmission backlashes and mechanical nonlinearities. This paper presents a innovative control strategy to mitigate these issues, achieved by robotically equipping the devices with encoders to directly monitor the output shaft of each actuator. Utilizing measured encoder data, this approach implements a model-free flatness-based control algorithm, specifically targeting high precision joint motion. The study details the development of a robust flatness-based feedback controller, with experimental results validating the methodology's effectiveness in eliminating backlashes, mechanical nonlinearities, position deviations to satisfy tracking requirements.

This analysis examines the complex relationship between multiple health outcomes, clinical characteristics, and health trajectories for patients with myocardial infarction (MI). We constructed and evaluated a data set for a MI-based acute care quality improvement initiative, focusing on patients admitted between 2012 and 2014. The dataset encompasses 16 patient-level variables, including demographics, comorbidities, and clinical factors, alongside three patient-specific outcomes: length of stay, occurrence of post-hospital mortality, and discharge status. To address these multiple outcomes, we employed a continuous-time, multi-state model that represents patient health courses as a network of states and transitions. Specifically, three primary trajectories were identified: (1) an "acute care" state encompassing the hospitalization period, (2) a "mortality" state entered upon death within the follow-up period, and (iii) a "nursing home" state entered upon placement in a nursing facility around discharge. By modeling the expected durations for each of these trajectories relative to the full follow-up window, we evaluated the impact of patient-specific covariates on multiple health outcomes. Results indicate that the health trajectories for patients with MI are strongly predicted by comorbidities and functional status. Consequently, this multi-state approach proves effective for analyzing multidimensional patient courses and the interplay of comorbidities and health trajectories.

**Introduction:**
Labeling data is a costly endeavor, particularly within medical imaging, where expert clinicians are required. Consequently, discrepancies between labels and ground-truth diagnoses are inevitable, leading to suboptimal model training. While statistical techniques aim to optimize data labeling, they often incur prohibitive costs.

**Problem & Solution:**
To address this, we introduce a cost-effective method that leverages Bayesian statistics to refurbish labels, enhancing the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in classification tasks. Our approach estimates the probability distribution of a label given an input image, allowing the model to assign higher confidence to correct labels and appropriately devalue incorrect ones.

**Experiments:**
We evaluated the efficacy of this strategy on benchmark datasets, including Kaggle's Dermatology dataset and a multi-class classification set comprising 11 distinct CT scan categories.

**Results:**
Our analysis demonstrates that confidence scores generated by our model align well with actual correct classification rates. Furthermore, this mechanism mitigates the negative impact of labeling errors, enabling superior overall model accuracy without requiring expensive post-hoc processes such as hard-mining strategies.

Topological phases of matter are often defined by the breaking and protecting of various symmetries. Hofstadter-type quantum Hall states, established by strong magnetic flux, are nontopological in normal circumstances. Nevertheless, it is demonstrated that strong-coupling Wilson-Dirac semimetals can be driven into a novel state: a Weyl semimetal that breaks time-reversal symmetry yet remains in the Hofstadter limit characterized by a strongly non-rational flux. In this phase, the system hosts pairs of topologically protected, chirally distinct Weyl nodes, analogous to a quantum Hall state. Notably, strong-coupling allows for the precise analytical determination of the phase diagram, revealing that this regime is highly accessible in existing experiments with Hofstadter superlattices.

To achieve a narrow emission line, high radiative purity, and intense, highly directional light, hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantennas are proposed. These structures are optimized using the hybrid Green's function technique, followed by simulation of a coupled plasmonic-resonant antenna system incorporating a point dipole. The results demonstrate that such antennas produce significantly higher and more directional far-field radiation compared to standard gold-on-silicon-on-insulator plasmonic antennas with diameters around 200 nm. Specifically, their performance surpasses that of standard plasmonic antennas with equivalent effective indices, while also showing superiority over Lumerical's standard dipole-on-dimer configurations. The study highlights how the strategic use of an optical cavity mode within the plasmonic element enables strong Purcell enhancement and efficient light-matter interaction. In addition to these findings, the work presents novel insights into the tradeoffs between radiative purity and directionality in nanophotonic systems, which could impact the design of quantum information devices.

In dense suspensions containing particles with finite size, a phenomenon known as anomalous screening occurs, causing effective charges and their associated electric fields, as well as long-range orientational correlations among prolate particles, to decay more rapidly than predicted by the standard Debye length. While the studies support the core principles of the anomalous screening hypothesis, discrepancies remain regarding the precise decay mechanisms. Additionally, it is demonstrated that even minute deviations from an ideal nematic alignment are sufficient to eliminate anomalous screening effects.

Sgr A East, a young and luminous supernova remnant (SNR) situated near the Galactic Center, is expanding rapidly and interacting with the region's dense interstellar medium. By utilizing high-resolution X-ray imaging and spectroscopy from Chandra, we analyzed this system to determine where the explosion originally occurred. Our findings demonstrate that the current position of the SNR's center lies approximately 1.5 parsecs from the Galactic Center. Furthermore, we observe that the center of the SNR shifts systematically along a trajectory toward the center of the region on a scale of roughly 100 kiloparsecs. Based on these observations, we model the explosion as a Type II supernova that originated near a massive star cluster known as AGCL1. Our results indicate that the progenitor star was located about 1.6 arcminutes, or approximately 4.4 arcminutes, south-west of the SNR's present-day center.

Synthetic Minority OverSampling Technique (SMOTe) methods are widely recognized for enhancing imbalanced datasets. While research has primarily focused on applying these techniques to two-class problems, this paper demonstrates that SMOTe variants can be effectively extended to multi-class scenarios. A framework for adapting these methods is presented, followed by an empirical evaluation of the candidate algorithms across several publicly available multi-class text classification datasets featuring eight, sixteen, and twenty-four distinct labels. Results indicate that the proposed generalization improves the performance of two of three implemented SMOTe ways. Finally, a newly developed two-parameter variant is introduced, achieving superior outcomes compared to existing algorithms.

Local news outlets have always been the primary source of information for individuals about events in their communities, a role that became even more critical with the spread of the pandemic. Although recent attention has largely focused on national media coverage of COVID-19, the impact of the disease is felt most intensely at the community level. This study examines how local media attention correlates with infection and death rates, as well as online audience engagement, from January to December 2020. Using Twitter data collected from 100 news sources across 100 U.S. cities, the analysis reveals a strong positive link between coverage intensity and case/death rates as well as audience engagement of events in their communities. This contradiction suggests that while the exact mechanisms driving this relationship require further investigation, this is a crucial insight given the potential consequences of media coverage on public behavior and information dissemination.

The computational efficiency of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) stems from its ability to approximate interactions between distant particle groups by treating them as multipole sources, a technique originally rooted in classical electrodynamics and later expanded for general physics $\boldsymbol{n}$-th order multipole sources conserve total angular momentum; however, lower-order multipoles fail to preserve this conservation. To address this limitation, a multipole model is introduced to maintain conservation of angular momentum while maintaining computational efficiency. Although this solution is derived specifically for the magnetization within FMMS, the methodology remains generalizable to other force models that possess conservation of angular momentum.

The phenomenon of polarization $K$-dependence in elastic $e^- \vec{p} \to e^- \vec{p}$ interactions constitutes a secondary observable at JLab, manifesting as the vector part of a generalized form factor combination. This study evaluates such dependencies for a $1\text{ GeV}$ incident electron beam, incorporating effects from both $^{14}$N impurities and nuclear corrections relative to a free proton model. Our findings indicate that this observable is relatively insensitive to nitrogen contamination, maintaining stability across impurity concentrations up to at least 10%. However, discrepancies between results derived from two non-empirical nuclear models exceed our current theoretical error margins. Ultimately, this analysis aims to facilitate the interpretation of future high-polarization data collected at JLab.

We introduce a process for enhancing data augmentation designed to support the efficient acquisition of competencies by parametric neural network-based experts within a set of specialists framework. This method enhances the efficacy with which each individual expert acquires its specific skill. Furthermore, the augmentation process serves to increase the versatility of experts trained using a limited volume of rehearsal data through dynamic data enhancement during inference. We demonstrate the method across multiple tasks, including those involving the mastery of distinct object properties and the acquisition of motor abilities.

This study details a search for Higgs boson pair ($HH$) production alongside a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) in the fully hadronic final state. The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision datasets from the ATLAS detector at the LHC, acquired at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV in 2015 and 2016, with integrated luminosities of $~140$ fb$^{-1}$ and $\sim$ 260 fb$^{-1}$, respectively. The signal extraction employs a multivariate technique based on a boosted decision tree. It is established that humans process negative statements by integrating prior knowledge with linguistic negators. We examine how the primordial features present in inflationary cosmology can mimic the effects of a particle collider operating at energies comparable to the cosmological horizon. Our analysis demonstrates that these physical imprints are not universal; rather, they are determined by the specific nature of the interacting fields, the character of the initial features, and the energy scales involved. Conversely, light fields produce a characteristic "swamp" signal shaped by the original features, leaving a phase-dependent signature that differentiates the two regimes. We also analyze the specific cases of massive scalar and vector perturbations, showing that even when initial conditions are confined to a narrow region, these phenomena can alter the statistical properties of the resulting scalar perturbations. Additionally, we explore how such effects can serve as a diagnostic tool to pinpoint the origin of a transition to inflation.

This paper investigates the role of phonon-mediated interactions in condensed matter physics using a Holstein-type model tailored for cuprates. These points are then linked via an advanced interpolation technique to form a vertebrae-cavity-curve (VCC) slice-by-slice. Subsequently, anatomical constraints are applied along the VCC to estimate the corresponding centers for difficult cases where localization might fail. A dedicated intervertebral segmentation algorithm is employed to segment each vertebra around the primary curve. Subsequent steps involve optimizing the vertebrae's boundaries according to their shape model and ensuring these estimations align with the longitudinal spine anatomy. Finally, identification is performed using the adapted localization centers as inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that this anatomically and model-constrained framework significantly improves robustness compared to existing techniques, achieving a 99.8% success rate in handling the slice slices that previously posed challenges.

Since the PPT condition is a necessary and sufficient indicator of separability for bipartite systems of two qubits, VOSO guarantees full accuracy within this dimensionality. For higher-dimensional systems, while the PPT rule remains necessary, it is no longer sufficient; thus, VOSO's output must be interpreted as a variable-phase approximation, providing a deterministic lower limit and stochastic upper limit values for entanglement. We demonstrate that the PPT energy convergence profile under VOSO supervision mirrors that observed during the minimization of the NPT value in the Variational Separability Algorithm (VSA). Electrostatic tearing modes in collisionless slab plasmas are examined through the lens of perturbed Vlasov-Maxwell theory, with the perturbed distribution function derived using a generalized drift kinetic equation. Within this framework, the Equation for the Perturbed Distribution Function (EPDF) undergoes significant simplification by eliminating the parallel velocity component. A critical aspect of this derivation is the incorporation of parallel magnetic curvature, which is essential for driving the tearing mode instability. We demonstrate that the general dynamics of electrostatic modes can be cast into the simplified form of the EPDF equation by appropriately selecting gauge terms. To solve these modes, an integral equation method is developed, which yields analytical estimates for both the growth rate and the imaginary component of the mode frequency. A notable advantage of this technique is that it avoids the need to calculate the perturbed distribution function directly. Furthermore, by selecting a Maxwellian equilibrium distribution modified with an anisotropy factor, specific estimates for growth rates and frequency components are calculated. The resulting analysis demonstrates that curvature-driven electrostatic tearing modes in slab plasmas exhibit much slower growth rates compared to their magnetic counterparts found in weakly collisionless environments.

This article addresses feature-level attribute manipulation (AM) specifically for fashion-image retrieval, aiming to generate altered image versions that match target attributes while optimizing further retrieval performance. We propose a semi-supervised framework that first trains a joint model to simultaneously handle image and attribute classification, which is subsequently utilized for the actual manipulation task. We also introduce a novel loss function to enhance the model's semi-supervised performance. Experiments on two major datasets, a newly created one, and another established one, demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over current state-of-the-art methods.

This work examines heuristic dual gradient flow methods designed to solve linear ill-posed equations within Banach spaces, specifically focusing on the identification of global errors and error estimates regarding solution representations. Initially, we demonstrate that these naturally occurring flows yield accurate solutions only if starting from a sufficiently well-behaved initial state; otherwise, they diverge rapidly. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a time-dependent regularization framework utilizing a strongly dissipative operator, proving that it generates stable evolution trajectories. Under appropriate conditions, this regularized dynamics converge toward outcomes derived from traditional approaches, such as Tikhonov-Morozov iterative solutions. Specifically, when initialized with weakly convergent sequences, the global errors follow predictable asymptotic behaviors, allowing for effective control mechanisms. Finally, we empirically validate our findings through numerical experiments addressing classical ill-posed challenges, including deconvolution and image reconstruction tasks.

We present advancements in the rapid joint computation of depth and light-radiance from multi-view images, a challenge known as super-resolution depth light-field estimation. Previous approaches often process depth values from all light rays uniformly, disregarding the fact that some rays are obstructed. Consequently, these constructs waste computational resources on invalid data regarding occluded regions while potentially introducing erroneous depth values for blocked areas. To address these shortcomings, we introduce an occlusion-aware cost constructor that dynamically adjusts calculations based on ray availability. By precisely accounting for occlusion, this method not only accelerates the estimation workflow but also enhances the overall depth solution's quality by correctly handling occluded regions where applicable. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm superior performance compared to existing methods, exhibiting a notably reduced computation time. Additionally, we have made this code publicly accessible.

Using the bilinear method, this study examines the Fokas-Lenells equations. We linearize the irreducible rational solutions corresponding to specific nonlinear equations within this system and utilize them with the D-differential operator method to construct a class of exact solutions. These solutions include algebro-geometric waves of the primary type II variant, a broad family of breathers, an optical soliton, a bright solitary wave, and limiting procedures of the latter two (saturating and dark solitary wave, respectively). Additionally, we analyze the behavior of these solutions within specific limits to derive another type of algebraic geometric solution and a dark-type breather, as well as the dark solitary wave and its limit states, respectively.

Non-Riemannian gravity theories have recently attracted significant interest as a potential foundation for quantum gravity and a framework to understand non-commutative spacetime at the Planck scale. Within double field theory (DBT)—a unified formalism for string theory that expands the dimensionality of spacelike fields beyond ten—we derive effective low-energy effective gravity actions that exhibit various degrees of non-Riemannian behavior. These actions emerge from DBT double labels written in chiral forms via projection operators; specifically, one such action corresponds to the theory of projectively special non-Riemannian gravity. By investigating the low-energy expansions of these actions, the study provides concrete examples for future theoretical and phenomenological scrutiny.

In home WiFi environments, users often utilize access points (APs) and extenders to boost coverage, yet the networks may operate in suboptimal conditions due to AP/Extender (AP/E) choice and channel congestion. To address this, the paper presents a comprehensive solution based on IEEE 802.11k/v standards for selecting appropriate APs and channelling strategies within residential setups. This research introduces a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) approach to train models that identify superior configurations through extensive simulation. Validations confirm that the proposed framework enhances both AP selection and channel assignment performance, delivering notable gains in evaluation metrics compared to existing methodologies.
